lesson.title: Carbohydrates: Sugar Chemistry as Fuel, Scaffold, and Signal
lesson.summary: Carbohydrates are a family of molecules built from carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in roughly a 1:2:1 ratio, and their many hydroxyl groups make them the cell's go to tools for energy storage, structural support, and molecular identification.
lesson.body:
When you hear the word carbohydrate, you probably think of bread, pasta, or table sugar, and you would not be wrong. At the molecular level, carbohydrates are compounds built almost entirely from carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, usually near a ratio of one carbon to two hydrogens to one oxygen, which is where the name carbo-hydrate, literally hydrated carbon, comes from. What makes this class biologically important is not the ratio itself but the functional groups it implies: every carbohydrate carries multiple hydroxyl groups (-OH) along its carbon backbone, plus at least one carbonyl group (C=O), an aldehyde or a ketone. Functional groups are the reactive, polar attachments that give an otherwise unreactive hydrocarbon chain its chemistry, and in carbohydrates those hydroxyl groups make sugars water soluble and ready to react with one another.

Carbohydrates are also a textbook case of the polymer and monomer relationship running through biochemistry. The monomer, or single repeating unit, of a carbohydrate is a monosaccharide, a simple sugar such as glucose. When two or more monosaccharides link together, they form a polymer: a disaccharide for two units, or a polysaccharide for hundreds or thousands of units, such as starch or cellulose. This monomer to polymer logic is identical to how amino acids build proteins or nucleotides build DNA, just with sugars instead.

The chemistry that links monosaccharides together is condensation, also called dehydration synthesis. When two sugar molecules bond, a hydroxyl group from one and a hydrogen from the other are removed and combined into a water molecule, while the two sugars become joined by a new covalent linkage called a glycosidic bond. This is the same reaction that assembles every biological polymer: monomers are stitched together and water is released as a byproduct. Running that reaction in reverse is hydrolysis, where a water molecule is added back across the bond, splitting the polymer apart, exactly what happens when you digest bread: enzymes in your saliva and small intestine hydrolyze the glycosidic bonds in starch, releasing free glucose your cells absorb and burn for energy.

Biologically, carbohydrates serve three broad roles. First is energy: glucose is the single most important fuel molecule for most cells, broken down through cellular respiration to generate ATP, and organisms store extra glucose in compact polymer form, as starch in plants or glycogen in animals. Second is structure: carbohydrate polymers like the cellulose in plant cell walls or the chitin in insect exoskeletons are built for mechanical strength rather than easy digestion. Third, and less obvious, is recognition: short carbohydrate chains attached to proteins or lipids on a cell's outer surface act like molecular name tags, letting your immune system distinguish your own cells from invaders and giving red blood cells their A, B, or O blood type identity.

That all three jobs trace back to the same simple chemistry: hydroxyl groups everywhere. A hydroxyl rich molecule like glucose is intensely hydrophilic, dissolving readily in cytoplasm and blood plasma, ideal for fast transport and metabolism. But change the geometry of the glycosidic bonds linking those same glucose units, as happens in cellulose versus starch, and you get a rigid, water insoluble fiber instead of an easily digested energy reserve. The sections that follow unpack how monosaccharides are built, how they link into disaccharides and polysaccharides, and why the shape of a glycosidic bond changes a carbohydrate's entire biological role.
